newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: U.N. envoy sees hope in talks with Kabul rulers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy sees hope in talks with Kabul rulers.

text.p: United Nations' special envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl said on Sunday he saw hopeful signs in talks with Kabul's new hardline Islamist rulers on issues such as whether women can work.
The Taleban, the two-year-old militia which took Kabul on Friday with barely a shot fired, has told men to report to work as usual but said women should stay at home.

The United Nations employs many women in its programmes in war-ravaged Afghanistan and has already suspended educational activities in areas previously captured by the Taleban, a militant Sunni Moslem movement which grew out of religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan.
Holl said he had discussed the role of women along with human rights in a two-hour meeting with the Taleban interim shura, or council.

"This is an issue and will remain an issue," he told a news conference. "I hope this does not remain a dialogue with both sides sitting on principles. I hope we can find some practical solutions. I had indications for some hope." Holl refused to elaborate.
About 70 percent of teachers in Kabul are women. Taleban fighters have entered foreign relief agencies in the capital to find out if women are working there, aid workers said.
Holl refused to say whether he had raised the issue of the execution of former president Najibullah, whose Soviet-backed regime encouraged women to get an education.
The U.N. envoy has already expressed his deep dismay at the execution. The U.N. Security Council late on Saturday deplored the "brutal execution" of Najibullah.
Almost the first act of Taleban on entering Kabul was to snatch Najibullah from the U.N. compound where he had stayed since anti-communist Mujahideen guerrillas took over the capital in April 1992.
His bloodied body, along with that of his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai, was hanged near the presidential palace from where he had fought the Mujahideen.

Holl said he would go to the northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif soon to talk to powerful Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who has his own army and small air force, in pursuit of national reconciliation.

He said he would also talk to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and his military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, who gave up Kabul without a fight and fled north to Panjsher valley, if they contacted him.
Rabbani, speaking from north Afghanistan, has urged Afghans to resist the Taleban, whom he described as puppets.
The deposed president has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban, a charge denied by Islamabad.
Two Pakistan foreign ministry officials held talks with Taleban leaders in Kabul on Sunday and discussed reopening the Pakistan embassy, sacked by anti-Pakistan protesters a year ago.

Ministry official Arif Ayub told Reuters Pakistan did not need to extend formal recognition to the Taleban government. "We recognise states, not governments, and we will deal with whatever government is in power," he said.

He said his government favoured an intra-Afghan dialogue between all factions, including those in the defeated former government, and was urging the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban to establish a broadbased administration.

Previously such calls have come to nothing and there was no indication whether the Taleban would talk to Masood or would continue a campaign that has brought it control of most of Afghanistan. Taleban has said it wants talks with Dostum.

After taking the capital, the Islamic militia has paused in its pursuit of forces loyal to the ousted president, who were apparently regrouping in Panjsher valley, which controls a vital section of the north-south Salang highway, a major Soviet supply route in the 1980s.
Instead it has concentrated on consolidating its hold over Kabul, where it quickly imposed strict fundamentalist law, promising death for adulterers and drinkers.
Holl said he had asked the Taleban to protect U.N. agencies working in Afghanistan and to respect the U.N. charter.

Asked why the United Nations wanted to increase cooperation with the secretive Taleban, Holl said: "Because the United Nations believes that without the cooperation of Taleban the Afghan issue cannot be solved."
The International Red Cross said on Sunday it had arranged a 35-lorry convoy of food and medical supplies in Pakistan to be sent to Kabul, probably on Monday.
Asian countries and commentators called at the weekend for an end to the fighting in Afghanistan, but nations generally stopped short of immediately recognising the new Taleban administration.
